title: Observability: metrics, traces, dashboards and SLOs
summary: Counters, gauges, histograms and spans; how histogram_quantile interpolates and how far off it can be; why labels, not samples, drive the bill; and SLOs with burn-rate alerts.
outcomes: Explain which questions metrics, traces and logs can each answer, and which they cannot
Compute a classic histogram quantile by hand and bound the error that bucket choice causes
Explain why averaging per-instance quantiles is wrong, and aggregate bucket counters instead
Count the time series a labelled histogram creates and predict a cardinality blow-up
Compute burn rates and error budget spend, and lay out a dashboard that answers incident questions

lessons.title: What metrics, traces and logs can each answer

blocks.md:
At 03:12 the pager fires. The checkout service's 99th percentile latency has gone from 180 ms to 1.3 s. You open a browser and you have exactly the telemetry you decided to collect weeks ago, no more.

That is the whole subject of this course. Observability is not a product you buy; it is the shape of the data you chose to keep. Different shapes answer different questions, and during an incident you cannot go back and change the shape.

You already know from the tail latency course that the mean hides the requests users remember, and from the microbenchmarking course that a number without a stated measurement model is not evidence. Both lessons apply here, at the scale of a whole system.

OpenTelemetry calls the kinds of telemetry *signals*. The three you will meet constantly are metrics, traces and logs.

A **metric** is a number accumulated or sampled over time and stored as a *time series*: a metric name, a set of label key-value pairs, and a stream of (timestamp, value) pairs. Every request contributes to it, but the request's identity is gone. Metrics are cheap per request and expensive per distinct label combination.

A **trace** follows one request across processes. It is a tree of *spans*, where each span is one operation and records its parent, so the tree shows what waited on what. Traces carry per-request detail, which is why they are almost always sampled.

A **log** is a timestamped record of a single event, with whatever fields you put in it. Logs carry the highest-cardinality detail (which account, which SQL statement) and cost the most per event.

scenes.caption: One checkout request crosses six components. Each one can emit all three signals, and each signal shows a different slice of this picture.
Metrics: one aggregate per component per scrape. You can see that payments and the database are slow in the same minute, but no metric says that this payments call waited on that query.
A trace follows one request and records parent and child spans, so the 1.21 s inside payments is visibly 0.90 s of waiting on the orders database. One request, not an average.
Logs: one record per event. The payments log line names the lock it waited on and the account involved, detail that no metric label should ever carry.
The triage order follows the signals: metrics say whether users are hurt and where, a trace says which hop inside one request, a log says exactly what that hop did.

blocks.md: The shape of the data decides which questions you can ask. Metrics answer "how often, how slow, for everyone". Traces answer "where did the time go inside this one request". Logs answer "what exactly happened at this instant".

Put the limits plainly.

- Metrics **cannot** tell you that one specific request was slow because of one specific downstream call. Two percentiles rising together is a correlation, and the two percentiles may even be computed over disjoint sets of requests.
- Traces **cannot** give you an exact rate, because they are sampled. A trace count is a sample count, and turning it back into a request rate means knowing the sampling probability.
- Logs **can** answer almost anything, which is why logging every field of every request is the most expensive mistake in this list.

A common misconception: "we log everything, so we are observable". Logs scale with traffic times fields per event, metrics scale with the number of distinct label combinations, and traces scale with the sampling rate. Choosing where each fact lives is the design work.

blocks.question: Checkout p99 reads 1.3 s and the orders database p99 reads 0.9 s, both rising in the same minute. What do the metrics alone establish?
options: That checkout requests are waiting on the database
That the database is the root cause, since it is the deepest component
That the two are correlated in time, but not that any single checkout request waited on the database
Nothing, because percentiles from different services are never comparable
blocks.explain: Metrics are per-component aggregates with no request identity, so simultaneity is a hypothesis, not a causal link. The slow checkout requests and the slow queries may even be disjoint sets. A trace carries parent and child spans and settles it for one request.

blocks.question: Which question can a sampled trace answer that a metric cannot answer even in principle?
options: How many requests per second the service handled
Where the time went inside one specific slow request
What fraction of requests exceeded 900 ms over the last 30 days
Whether the error rate is rising
blocks.explain: The other three are ratios or rates over all requests, which is exactly what metrics are for and what sampled traces are bad at. Only the trace keeps the causal structure of an individual request: which child span held the parent open and for how long.

lessons.title: Counters, gauges, histograms, and the quantile you must not average

blocks.md:
Prometheus defines four metric types, and the choice is not cosmetic: it decides what you are allowed to compute later.

A **counter** is cumulative and monotonically increasing. The docs are explicit that its value can only go up, or reset to zero on restart, and that it should not be used for values that can decrease. It produces a single float time series.

A **gauge** is a single numerical value that can rise and fall: queue depth, in-flight requests, free bytes. Also one series.

Why prefer a counter over a gauge for "requests per second"? Because a counter is robust to missed scrapes. If your collector misses two scrapes, a gauge of "requests in the last interval" loses those requests forever, while the counter still carries them: you recover the rate by differencing.

You never graph a counter directly. You apply `rate()`, which, in the words of the PromQL docs, automatically adjusts for breaks in monotonicity such as counter resets due to target restarts.

blocks.title: A counter, eight scrapes, one restart

scenes.caption: Eight scrapes of http_requests_total, 15 s apart. A counter only moves up, so each scrape is a running total since process start, never a rate.
Scrape 5 reads 12, far below the 1120 before it. The process restarted and the counter began again at zero. This is the one legal way a counter goes down.
rate() differences consecutive samples and, on a break in monotonicity, treats the new value as the increase since the reset: 1120 then 12 contributes 12, not minus 1108.
Total increase over the window is 193 requests in 105 s, about 1.84 requests per second. Subtracting first from last would have reported minus 8.8 per second.

blocks.caption: The 12 is the post-restart value, used as the increase across the reset. Real rate() also extrapolates slightly to the window edges; the arithmetic above is the idea without that correction.

blocks.md: Never compute a rate as last value minus first value over a counter. One restart in the window turns a positive rate into a large negative number, and `rate()` exists precisely to handle that case for you.

blocks.caption: What a classic histogram looks like on the /metrics endpoint after 100 requests. The bucket counts are cumulative, so each one includes the ones before it.
blocks.code:
# HELP http_request_duration_seconds Request duration.
# TYPE http_request_duration_seconds histogram
http_request_duration_seconds_bucket{le="0.05"}  10
http_request_duration_seconds_bucket{le="0.1"}   60
http_request_duration_seconds_bucket{le="0.25"}  90
http_request_duration_seconds_bucket{le="0.5"}   97
http_request_duration_seconds_bucket{le="1.0"}  100
http_request_duration_seconds_bucket{le="+Inf"} 100
http_request_duration_seconds_sum              13.6
http_request_duration_seconds_count             100

blocks.md:
A **summary** also tracks count and sum, but it computes configurable quantiles inside the instrumented process over a sliding time window, exposing `<name>{quantile="0.95"}` and friends.

That sounds convenient and it is a trap. The quantiles and the window are fixed at instrumentation time, so you cannot ask for p99.9 later without a redeploy. Observation is relatively expensive because of the streaming quantile computation. And the Prometheus docs list summaries flatly as "Not aggregatable". OpenTelemetry's metrics data model agrees, marking Summary as legacy and noting that summary points cannot always be merged in a meaningful way.

Why can a precomputed quantile not be aggregated? Because a quantile is a position in a distribution, and positions do not add. Only counts add.

This is the same point Gil Tene makes in [How NOT to Measure Latency](https://www.infoq.com/presentations/latency-response-time/): a percentile is a property of a specific set of measurements, and arithmetic on percentiles from different sets is not arithmetic on anything.

blocks.prompt: Instance A served 1900 requests, all exactly 50 ms. Instance B served 100 requests, all exactly 2000 ms. Your panel shows the average of the two reported p95 values. Is it above or below the true p95 of the 2000 pooled requests, and by how much?
blocks.reveal:
Instance A's p95 is 50 ms; instance B's p95 is 2000 ms; their average is **1025 ms**.

Pool the 2000 requests: 1900 at 50 ms, then 100 at 2000 ms. The nearest-rank p95 is the 1900th value, which is **50 ms**.

The panel reads 20.5 times the truth, and it reads 1025 ms when no single request ever took 1025 ms. The error comes entirely from the traffic imbalance: averaging gave the 100-request instance the same weight as the 1900-request one.

blocks.title: Average of per-instance p95 against the real p95

scenes.caption: Traffic imbalance. A: 1900 requests at 50 ms. B: 100 requests at 2000 ms. The average of the two p95 values is 1025 ms; the pooled p95 is 50 ms, a factor of 20.5 out.
Equal traffic, different shapes. A: 900 at 40 ms plus 100 at 120 ms. B: 900 at 40 ms, 50 at 200 ms, 50 at 900 ms. The average still overstates: 160 ms against a true 120 ms.
Same two instances, now at p99: 120 ms and 900 ms average to 510 ms, while the pooled p99 is 900 ms. The error has no fixed sign, so you cannot even correct for it.

blocks.md: The fix is to aggregate the thing that adds. Bucket counters add, so you sum the bucket counters across instances first, keeping the `le` label, and estimate the quantile once at the end. The Prometheus docs call averaging the quantiles of a summary "statistically nonsensical values" and give exactly this replacement.

blocks.caption: The wrong panel and the right one. Note that le must survive the by clause, because the quantile estimator needs the whole cumulative curve.
blocks.code:
# wrong: the mean of 50 precomputed p95 values
avg(http_request_duration_seconds{quantile="0.95"})

# right: add the bucket counters first, estimate once
histogram_quantile(
  0.95,
  sum by (le) (rate(http_request_duration_seconds_bucket[5m]))
)

blocks.md: Counts aggregate; quantiles do not. If you want to compute a percentile across instances, regions or time windows later, you must store counts per bucket now. That single decision is why histograms beat summaries almost everywhere.

blocks.question: A service runs on 50 pods, each exporting a summary with quantile 0.95. The dashboard shows avg of those 50 values. One pod is slow. What is wrong with the panel?
options: Nothing: averaging per-pod p95 values is the standard aggregation
It should use max instead, which is the correct aggregate for a quantile
It is only wrong when the pods receive different amounts of traffic
The average of 50 p95 values is not the p95 of the pooled requests, and the error can go in either direction
blocks.explain: Quantiles are positions in a distribution, so they do not combine by any arithmetic. Traffic imbalance makes the error worse, but the second figure scene showed equal traffic still giving 160 ms against a true 120 ms. max is an upper bound on the per-pod values, not the pooled p95 either.

blocks.question: You must report the fraction of requests served under 300 ms, and you want to be able to change that threshold later without redeploying the service. Which instrument?
options: A histogram with a boundary at 0.3, since stored bucket counts let the server compute any threshold that has a boundary
A summary configured with quantile 0.95
A gauge set to the duration of the last request
A counter incremented whenever a request finishes under 300 ms
blocks.explain: The counter answers today's question exactly but hard-codes 300 ms into the binary. The summary fixes the quantiles, not a threshold, at instrumentation time. The gauge throws away every request but the last. Only the histogram keeps counts you can query differently later, limited to the boundaries you chose.

lessons.title: Inside a classic histogram: buckets, cumulative counts, interpolation

blocks.md:
A classic histogram is a row of counters and nothing more. When the client records `observe(v)` it increments every bucket whose upper bound is greater than or equal to `v`, adds `v` to `_sum`, and adds 1 to `_count`.

That is the whole data structure. Everything you later call a percentile is reconstructed from those counts, and the reconstruction is where the error lives.

scenes.caption: Five bucket counters, a sum and a count, all starting at zero. The le label is the inclusive upper bound, and the counters are cumulative: le = 1 counts everything at or below 1 s.
observe(0.42): 0.42 is at or below 0.5, so every bucket from le = 0.5 upward gains 1 and the two below stay at zero. _sum gains 0.42, _count gains 1.
observe(0.08): now every bucket moves, because 0.08 is at or below all five bounds. Note that no bucket ever stores 0.08 itself; only the counts and the running sum know it happened.
observe(3.0): above every finite bound, so only le = +Inf moves. _count always equals the +Inf bucket. A request slower than your largest bucket is counted, but its duration is now invisible.

blocks.md:
Now the reconstruction. `histogram_quantile(phi, b)` takes a cumulative bucket vector and returns an estimate of the $\phi$-quantile. Reading the Prometheus source (`BucketQuantile` in `promql/quantile.go`) the algorithm is four lines:

1. `observations` is the count in the `+Inf` bucket, that is $N$.
2. `rank` is $\phi N$.
3. Binary-search the buckets, excluding `+Inf`, for the first one whose cumulative count is at or above `rank`. Call its index $b$.
4. Interpolate linearly between that bucket's bounds.

blocks.caption: The l values are bucket upper bounds and the C values are cumulative counts. For b = 0 the lower bound is taken as 0. This is the step that assumes a uniform distribution of observations inside the chosen bucket.

blocks.title: Finding p50, p90 and p99 in five buckets

scenes.caption: 100 requests, five finite buckets. The middle row is how many requests landed in each bucket; only the bottom row is actually stored, as six counters.
p50: rank is 0.5 x 100 = 50. The first cumulative count at or above 50 is 60 at le = 0.1. Interpolating inside (0.05, 0.1] with 40 of its 50 observations: 0.05 + 0.05 x (40/50) = 90 ms.
p90: rank 90. The first cumulative count at or above 90 is exactly 90 at le = 0.25, so the fraction is 30/30 and the estimate lands exactly on the boundary: 250 ms.
p99: rank 99. The first cumulative count at or above 99 is 100 at le = 1.0, so the chosen bucket is (0.5, 1.0], which holds 3 observations and needs 2 of them.

Those 3 requests actually took 0.52, 0.55 and 0.98 s, so the true p99 is 550 ms. The estimate of 833 ms is 51.5 percent high, and had they been 0.95, 0.96 and 0.99 s it would have been 13.2 percent low.

blocks.caption: The p99 arithmetic in full. The estimate is pinned inside (0.5, 1.0], so no interpolation rule can be wrong by more than that bucket's width, and none can do better either: the stored counts say nothing about where inside the bucket the three values sit.

blocks.md: Three rules from the docs and the source that bite in practice. The error is bounded by the width of the bucket the quantile falls in. The lowest bucket's lower bound is assumed to be 0 when that bucket's upper bound is above 0, and otherwise the function just returns that upper bound. If the rank falls in the `+Inf` bucket there is nothing to interpolate, so you get back the upper bound of the second-highest bucket, which looks like a suspiciously round constant on your graph.

blocks.prompt: The Go client's default buckets are 0.005, 0.01, 0.025, 0.05, 0.1, 0.25, 0.5, 1, 2.5, 5, 10 seconds. A service has a 60 ms median and a slow path near 800 ms. How wrong will the default-bucket p90 and p99 be?
blocks.reveal:
Measured on 10,000 simulated requests (95 percent lognormal around 60 ms, 5 percent lognormal around 800 ms):

- true p50 61.9 ms, estimate 67.2 ms, **+8.6 percent**
- true p90 124.3 ms, estimate 187.9 ms, **+51.2 percent**
- true p99 1048.7 ms, estimate 1309.5 ms, **+24.9 percent**

The p90 is the worst because the whole region from 100 ms to 250 ms is one bucket, and the default set has no boundary anywhere near 124 ms. The defaults are not wrong; they are a guess about a service you are not running.

scenes.caption: p99. Coarse buckets put the rank in (1, 10] and interpolate to 2857 ms, 172 percent high. The defaults give 1309 ms. Buckets placed around the observed slow path, with extra bounds just above the true p90 and p99, give 1059 ms against a true 1049 ms.
p90 is where coarse buckets fail hardest: the rank falls in (0.1, 1], a bucket 900 ms wide, so the estimate is 500 ms against a true 124 ms, 302 percent high.
p50 is easy for everyone, because half the mass sits in a narrow region that every bucket set resolves. Coarse buckets are even slightly low here, at 60 ms against 62 ms.

blocks.md:
Reading that figure the right way: the estimate is not noisy, it is *biased by your bucket layout*, and the bias is stable. A p90 panel reading 188 ms will read 188 ms all week while the real p90 is 124 ms.

How to choose boundaries. Put them where you intend to make decisions: at your SLO threshold, and spaced geometrically (each bound roughly 1.5x to 3x the previous one) across the range you actually serve. The SRE book makes the same recommendation, suggesting latency buckets roughly a factor of 3 apart. Then check the figure above against your own data rather than trusting the defaults.

blocks.caption: Aggregating classic histograms correctly: rate() each bucket counter, sum keeping le, then estimate. Classic histograms with different bucket boundaries are generally not aggregatable, so the boundaries must match across instances.
blocks.code:
# p99 across every instance of the service, last 5 minutes
histogram_quantile(
  0.99,
  sum by (le) (rate(http_request_duration_seconds_bucket[5m]))
)

# fraction of requests inside a 300 ms target, which needs a
# boundary at exactly le="0.3" to be answerable at all
sum(rate(http_request_duration_seconds_bucket{le="0.3"}[5m]))
  /
sum(rate(http_request_duration_seconds_count[5m]))

blocks.md: Prometheus now also offers **native histograms**, where you pick a resolution instead of boundaries and the buckets follow an exponential schema covering the whole range. The docs' advice is direct: if you can, use native histograms and prefer them over both classic histograms and summaries. Their buckets are always compatible with each other, so the aggregation problem disappears, and the error is bounded by the configured resolution rather than by a bucket you guessed years ago.

A classic histogram quantile is an interpolation inside one bucket. Its error is bounded by that bucket's width and nothing else, so a percentile panel is only as good as the boundary you placed next to the value you care about.

blocks.question: A classic histogram has bounds 0.1, 1, 10 and +Inf with cumulative counts 8300, 9874, 10000, 10000 out of 10000 observations. What does histogram_quantile(0.99, ...) return?
options: 10 s, the upper bound of the bucket where the rank falls
1 s, the upper bound of the bucket below the rank
2.857 s, interpolating linearly inside the 1 s to 10 s bucket
NaN, because no observations fall above 10 s
blocks.explain: The rank is 0.99 x 10000 = 9900. The first cumulative count at or above 9900 is 10000 at le = 10. Within that bucket the count is 10000 minus 9874 = 126 and the rank offset is 9900 minus 9874 = 26, so the estimate is 1 + 9 x (26/126) = 2.857 s. The true p99 of this data is 1049 ms.

blocks.question: Your p99 panel reads exactly 10.0 s minute after minute, and 10 is your largest finite bucket bound. What is the most likely explanation?
options: A counter reset corrupted the bucket counts
The rank falls in the +Inf bucket, so the function returns the second-highest bound
Requests really do take 10.0 s, consistently
histogram_quantile cannot interpolate in the top bucket and is returning NaN, rendered as 10
blocks.explain: More than 1 percent of requests are above 10 s, so the rank lands in the +Inf bucket. There is no finite upper bound to interpolate towards, and the documented behaviour is to return the upper bound of the second-highest bucket. A constant reading at a bucket boundary is the signature. The fix is a larger top bound, not a different query.

lessons.title: Cardinality: labels multiply, and a histogram multiplies again

blocks.md:
A time series is identified by its metric name plus its complete label set. The Prometheus naming guide states the consequence plainly: every unique combination of key-value label pairs represents a new time series.

That sentence is the entire cost model. A metric's cost does not scale with how many requests it observes; it scales with how many distinct label combinations exist. Ten billion requests through one unlabelled counter is still one series. Ten thousand requests through a counter labelled by user id is ten thousand series, forever, because the series keeps existing after the user leaves.

scenes.caption: A realistic label set for an HTTP counter: 4 methods, 20 route templates, 6 status classes, 50 instances. Each label looks small on its own.
They do not add, they multiply. Method times path is already 80 combinations.
Times status is 480, and times instance is 24,000 label sets for this one metric name.
Now make it a histogram. The Go client's default buckets give 11 finite bounds plus +Inf, that is 12 bucket series, plus _sum and _count: 14 series per label set, so 336,000 series.

blocks.caption: One metric name. The 14 is 12 bucket series (11 finite bounds plus +Inf) plus _sum and _count, which is what a Prometheus client histogram with default buckets produces per label set.

blocks.md:
Two consequences follow immediately.

First, a histogram is roughly an order of magnitude more expensive per label set than a counter. That is usually worth it, but it means the label set you would casually accept on a counter is the one you must argue about on a histogram.

Second, adding one label multiplies everything that came before it. Adding a `customer_id` with 200 values to this histogram does not add 200 series; it makes 67,200,000 of them.

blocks.title: Series for one metric as the route label grows

x.label: distinct values of the path label

scenes.caption: At 20 route templates, 50 instances and default buckets: 24,000 label sets, 336,000 histogram series against 24,000 for a plain counter.
Autoscale to 200 instances and nothing else changes, yet the histogram passes 1.3 million series. The instance label is multiplicative like every other label.
Back to 50 instances, now with one extra label of 200 values. The top curve is the same metric at 67 million series. This is how a monitoring system falls over in an afternoon.

blocks.md: Never put an unbounded set in a label. The naming guide names the usual offenders: do not use labels to store dimensions with high cardinality, such as user IDs, email addresses, or other unbounded sets of values. Raw URLs with query strings, trace ids, error message strings and timestamps belong on the same list.

blocks.caption: The same fact, kept in the right place. The path label uses the route template, not the request URI, so its cardinality is the number of routes you wrote, not the number of users you have.

blocks.md:
The practical guidance in the Prometheus instrumentation docs is blunt: try to keep the cardinality of your metrics below 10, and metrics above that should be limited to a handful across your whole system. If you have a metric with cardinality over 100, or one that can grow that large, consider other approaches. The vast majority of your metrics should have no labels at all.

The positive version of the rule: metrics carry the low-cardinality facts you want to aggregate (route, status class, region), traces and logs carry the high-cardinality facts you want to look up (order id, account, SQL text). Exemplars, which attach a trace id to a histogram bucket sample, are the bridge: a tiny number of trace ids per bucket rather than a label dimension.

blocks.question: You add a customer_id label with 200 values to the histogram above, which already has 24,000 label sets and 14 series per label set. How many series does that one metric become?
options: 336,200, since the new label adds 200 series
24,000, because labels do not change the series count
blocks.explain: Labels multiply: 24,000 x 200 = 4,800,000 label sets, each still producing 14 series, so 67,200,000. The 4,800,000 option is the label-set count, which is the number you get if you forget that a histogram costs 14 series per label set.

blocks.question: Which single change cuts the series count the most for a histogram with 11 finite buckets and 24,000 label sets?
options: Halving the number of buckets
Replacing the histogram with a summary exposing three quantiles
Dropping the instance label, 50 values, by aggregating before storage
Shortening the metric name
blocks.explain: Dropping a 50-value label divides the series count by 50. Halving the buckets takes 14 series per label set down to 8, under a factor of 2, and destroys the resolution you need for percentiles. A three-quantile summary is 5 series per label set rather than 14, a factor of under 3, and it costs you the ability to aggregate at all. The metric name has no effect on series count.

lessons.title: Traces: spans, context propagation, and what sampling throws away

blocks.md:
The OpenTelemetry specification's definition is one sentence: a Span represents a single operation within a trace. A span carries a name, an immutable span context, a parent (a span, a span context, or none), a kind, start and end timestamps, attributes, links, timestamped events and a status.

The spec is equally terse about the whole: a tree of related spans comprises a trace. Each trace has exactly one root span, every other span has exactly one parent, and all spans in a trace share one trace id. That parent pointer is the entire reason traces can answer causal questions that metrics cannot.

What must cross a process boundary is the **span context**: a 16-byte trace id with at least one non-zero byte, an 8-byte span id with at least one non-zero byte, trace flags (including the sampled bit), a trace state, and a flag saying whether this context arrived from a remote parent. Nothing else needs to travel.

This is the model Dapper introduced in 2010, which used probabilistically unique 64-bit integers for its span and trace ids and recorded a human-readable span name, a span id and a parent id for every unit of work.

scenes.caption: The root span. The gateway saw this request take 1300 ms, against a normal 180 ms. That is as much as the latency metric from lesson 1 told you.
The gateway's child span: checkout was busy for 1280 of the 1300 ms. The 20 ms difference is the gateway's own work plus two network hops.
Checkout's two children, in sequence: a 42 ms inventory call, then a 1210 ms payments call. The question has narrowed from six components to one.
Payments' child: one 900 ms query on the orders database, 69 percent of the user-visible 1300 ms. The other 310 ms inside payments is its own work plus waiting for a pooled connection.

Simplified: a real trace of this request would also show the pool wait as its own span, any retry, and client and server timestamps from different clocks, which is why span boundaries are bounded rather than exact.

blocks.md: Dapper's insight about these diagrams is worth repeating: a span can contain information from more than one host. Every RPC span records annotations from both the client and the server process, which makes two-host spans the most common kind. Because the two timestamps come from different clocks, Dapper's analysis tools used the fact that a client always sends before the server receives to put a lower and an upper bound on the server-side timestamps rather than trusting them outright.

How does the child process learn its parent? Through a **propagator**: an object that reads and writes context data to and from the messages applications exchange. It has two operations. `Inject` writes the current context into a carrier, such as an outgoing HTTP request's headers. `Extract` reads an incoming carrier and returns a new context. The spec's only defined propagator type is `TextMapPropagator`, which moves string key-value pairs.

The standard wire format is the W3C `traceparent` header: four dash-separated fields, with the trace id as 32 lowercase hex characters, the parent span id as 16, and two hex characters of flags whose least significant bit, `0x01`, is the sampled flag.

blocks.caption: The traceparent example from the W3C specification, with the fields named. The parent-id field is the caller's span id, which becomes this span's parent.
blocks.code:
traceparent: 00-4bf92f3577b34da6a3ce929d0e0e4736-00f067aa0ba902b7-01
             |  |                                |                |
             |  |                                |                flags: sampled = 0x01
             |  |                                parent span id: 16 hex (8 bytes)
             |  trace id: 32 hex (16 bytes)
             version: 00

scenes.caption: The gateway starts the root span and injects traceparent into the outgoing request. Ids are abbreviated here; a real trace id is 32 hex characters and a real span id 16.
Checkout extracts the context, sees a remote parent, and creates its own span with a fresh span id. The trace id it received is never changed.
Checkout injects again on the way out. The trace id is identical, the parent id is now checkout's own span id, and the sampled bit is still 01, so payments records too.
The same request with the sampled bit at 00. Under the default ParentBased sampler both downstream services drop their spans, so a trace is kept or dropped as a whole, never half of it.

blocks.md:
That last scene is the sampling mechanism. An OpenTelemetry `Sampler` is asked, just before a span is created, for a decision given the parent context, the trace id, the span name, the span kind, the initial attributes and the links. It returns one of three decisions:

- `DROP`: not recorded, events and attributes discarded.
- `RECORD_ONLY`: recorded locally, but the sampled flag must not be set.
- `RECORD_AND_SAMPLE`: recorded, and the sampled flag is set.

The built-in samplers include `AlwaysOn`, `AlwaysOff`, a trace-id ratio sampler, and `ParentBased`, a decorator that chooses a sampler based on whether a parent exists and whether it was remote. The spec's default is `ParentBased(root=AlwaysOn)`, and it requires the ratio decision to be a deterministic function of the trace id so that every service in a trace reaches the same answer.

blocks.prompt: Head sampling is on at 1 in 1024, Dapper's original rate. A bug affects 20 requests out of a million. What is the chance that at least one of those 20 requests left you a trace?
blocks.reveal:
$1 - (1 - 1/1024)^{20} = 0.0194$, that is **1.9 percent**.

At 1 in 100 it is 18.2 percent. At 1 in 10 it is 87.8 percent. Even at 1 in 1024 with a thousand affected requests out of a million, the chance is only 62.4 percent.

Head sampling is a lottery you enter before you know what the request will do, so rare events are exactly the ones it loses. That asymmetry is the whole argument for tail sampling.

blocks.caption: n is the number of affected requests and p the head sampling probability. The probability is driven by the product n times p, so halving the sampling rate on a rare bug is close to halving your chance of seeing it at all.

blocks.title: Chance a head sampler catches at least one bad request

y.label: probability of at least one trace

scenes.caption: At 1 in 1024 you need roughly 700 affected requests before the odds are even. A bug that hits 20 users is invisible.
At 1 in 100 the curve shifts left by a factor of 10: about 70 affected requests for even odds, and 18 percent at 20 requests.
At 1 in 10 you catch a 20-request bug 88 percent of the time, but you are now storing a tenth of all spans, which is the cost side of the trade.

blocks.md:
**Head sampling** decides as early as possible without inspecting the whole trace. It is cheap and easy to reason about, and its documented weakness is that it cannot base a decision on data from across the entire trace, so it cannot guarantee that traces containing an error are kept.

**Tail sampling** decides after the spans are complete, considering all or most of the spans in the trace. That buys you rules like "keep every trace with an error", "keep every trace over 1 s", and "sample the chatty health-check route at 1 in 10,000". The OpenTelemetry docs call it almost always necessary for large systems that must sample, and are equally clear about the cost: it needs stateful components that buffer large amounts of data, possibly dozens or hundreds of nodes, which must themselves be monitored and may have to fall back to simpler sampling under load. A common production shape is head sampling first, to protect the pipeline, then tail sampling before export.

Is tracing cheap enough to leave on? Dapper measured it. Root span creation and destruction averaged 204 nanoseconds, non-root spans 176 nanoseconds, and annotating a sampled span 40 nanoseconds, on a 2.2 GHz server. Each stored span averaged 426 bytes, and collection accounted for under 0.01 percent of network traffic, with the collector daemon never above 0.3 percent of one core.

And yet the sampling rate mattered: on a web search cluster, tracing every request cost 16.3 percent average latency, 1 in 16 cost 2.12 percent, and 1 in 1024 cost minus 0.20 percent, which is inside the stated 2.5 percent experimental error. Their conclusion was that trace sampling is indeed necessary to avoid noticeable latency degradation. The expensive part was never the span object; it was writing them all down.

A trace is kept or dropped as a whole, and the decision is made by whoever starts it. Head sampling trades away rare events; tail sampling buys them back with buffering and stateful collectors. Never read a trace count as a request count.

blocks.question: Head sampling at 1 in 100 is configured. An incident affects 5 requests. What is the chance you have a trace for at least one of them?
options: About 1 percent
About 50 percent
100 percent, because the trace-id hash is deterministic
About 5 percent
blocks.explain: $1 - 0.99^5 = 0.049$, about 5 percent. Determinism means every service in one trace agrees on the decision; it does not mean the decision favours the requests you later care about. For five affected requests you need tail sampling, or an always-on rule for errors.

blocks.question: Which setup guarantees a complete trace for every request that returned a 500?
options: Tail sampling in the collector, which buffers a trace's spans and decides once they are complete
Head sampling at 1 in 10 plus a longer retention period
A trace-id ratio sampler at 0.01, since its decision is deterministic
Setting the sampled bit at the gateway only when the gateway sees an error
blocks.explain: Only a decision made after the spans exist can condition on the error. Longer retention keeps dropped spans dropped. A deterministic ratio sampler is still a ratio. The last option fails because the gateway must inject traceparent before the request runs, so at decision time the error has not happened yet, and the downstream spans would already have been dropped.

lessons.title: SLOs, error budgets, burn-rate alerts, and the 03:00 dashboard

blocks.md:
Everything so far has been about measurement. This lesson is about deciding what counts as broken, which is the only way to get an alert that is worth waking someone for.

The SRE workbook defines a **service level indicator** as an indicator of the level of service you are providing, and recommends expressing it as a ratio: the number of good events divided by the total number of events. A **service level objective** sets a target level of reliability for that indicator. The **error budget** is the rest: the SLO is a target percentage and the error budget is 100 percent minus the SLO.

blocks.caption: A ratio SLI has a useful property: it is a counter divided by a counter, so it aggregates across instances and windows, unlike the quantiles of the previous lessons.

blocks.md:
Make it concrete with the checkout service from lesson 1. Two SLOs, both ratios over a rolling 30-day window:

- availability: 99.9 percent of requests return a non-5xx status;
- latency: 99 percent of requests complete within 900 ms, which is answerable only because there is a histogram bucket at `le="0.9"`.

At 2,000 requests per second, 30 days is 5,184,000,000 requests, so the availability budget is 5,184,000 failed requests. Read as time instead, 30 days is 43,200 minutes and 0.1 percent of that is **43.2 minutes** of total unavailability per month.

Now the number that makes alerting work. **Burn rate** is, in the workbook's words, how fast, relative to the SLO, the service consumes the error budget. Burn rate 1 means you will spend exactly the whole budget in exactly the window. Burn rate 10 means you will spend it in a tenth of the window.

Two lines of arithmetic follow from the definition, and they are all you need.

blocks.tex: \text{burn rate} = \frac{\text{observed error ratio}}{1 - \mathrm{SLO}}, \qquad \text{budget spent} = \text{burn rate}\times\frac{\text{window}}{\text{SLO period}}
blocks.caption: For a 99.9 percent SLO over 30 days: an error ratio of 1 percent is a burn rate of 10, and sustaining it for one hour spends 10 x 1/720 = 1.39 percent of the month's budget.

blocks.title: How long the budget lasts at a given burn rate

y.label: hours until the budget is gone

scenes.caption: A 30-day window. Burn rate 1 lasts 720 hours, burn rate 2 lasts 15 days, burn rate 10 lasts 3 days, and a full outage at a 99.9 percent SLO is burn rate 1000, which empties the budget in 43 minutes.
Shorten the window to 7 days and every burn rate becomes more urgent: the same burn rate 10 now exhausts the budget in 16.8 hours. The window is part of the SLO, not a reporting detail.

blocks.md: The point of the burn rate is that it converts "is this bad" into a number with a deadline, and it does so independently of traffic. A 2 percent error ratio is a burn rate of 20 whether you serve 20 requests per second or 20,000.

blocks.title: Four incidents, by burn rate and by budget spent

scenes.caption: Burn rate, against a 99.9 percent SLO. The 30-minute incident looks by far the worst: burn rate 20, twenty times the sustainable pace.
Percent of the 30-day budget actually spent. The burn-rate ranking inverts: the brief spike cost 1.39 percent, while the mild 12-hour drift cost 2.5 percent and the 4-hour one 2.78 percent.
Same thing in minutes of the 43.2-minute monthly budget. Both views matter: burn rate tells you how fast, budget spent tells you how much is left.

blocks.md:
That inversion is why a single threshold alert cannot work. Page on "error ratio above 1 percent" and you wake someone for a 10-second blip that cost 0.004 percent of the budget, while a quiet 0.15 percent drift eats the month unnoticed.

The workbook's recommendation is **multiwindow, multi-burn-rate alerting**. Each rule pairs a long window, which sets the burn rate you care about, with a short window at the same threshold, which makes the alert stop firing soon after the errors stop. An alert fires only when both windows are over the threshold.

The workbook's table for a 99.9 percent SLO, with the budget each rule lets you spend before it fires:

1. **page**: burn rate 14.4, long window 1 hour, short window 5 minutes, 2 percent of the budget.
2. **page**: burn rate 6, long window 6 hours, short window 30 minutes, 5 percent of the budget.
3. **ticket**: burn rate 1, long window 3 days, short window 6 hours, 10 percent of the budget.

Check the first row against the formula: $14.4 \times 1/720 = 0.02$. The threshold on the error ratio itself is the burn rate times the budget, so 14.4 x 0.001 = 1.44 percent, 0.6 percent, and 0.1 percent respectively.

blocks.caption: Each row of the table is the same identity read backwards: pick how much budget you are willing to spend before being told, pick a window, and the burn rate threshold falls out.
The three rules as recording-rule expressions. error_ratio:rateXX is a precomputed ratio of two counter rates, which is why the SLI had to be a ratio.
blocks.code:
# 99.9% availability SLO over 30 days, so 1 - SLO = 0.001

- alert: CheckoutBudgetFastBurn        # 2% of budget in 1h
  expr: error_ratio:rate1h  > 14.4 * 0.001
    and error_ratio:rate5m  > 14.4 * 0.001

- alert: CheckoutBudgetSlowBurn        # 5% of budget in 6h
  expr: error_ratio:rate6h  > 6 * 0.001
    and error_ratio:rate30m > 6 * 0.001

- alert: CheckoutBudgetTicket          # 10% of budget in 3d
  expr: error_ratio:rate3d > 1 * 0.001
    and error_ratio:rate6h > 1 * 0.001

blocks.prompt: The error ratio settles at 0.15 percent and stays there. Which of the three rules fire, and when?
blocks.reveal:
Burn rate is 0.0015 / 0.001 = **1.5**.

- Fast-burn page needs 1.44 percent: never fires.
- Slow-burn page needs 0.6 percent: never fires.
- Ticket needs both the 6-hour and the 3-day ratio above 0.1 percent. The 6-hour average crosses 0.1 percent after 4 hours, but the 3-day average starts at zero and only reaches 0.1 percent once 0.0015 x t/72 > 0.001, that is after **t = 48 hours**.

So a steady 1.5x burn produces no page and a ticket two days later, having spent 1.5 x 48/720 = 10 percent of the month. That is the design working as intended, not a bug.

blocks.md: Alert on symptoms, not causes. The SRE book's advice is to focus much more effort on catching symptoms than causes, and to worry about a cause only when it is very definite and very imminent. A page saying "cache hit rate dropped" is a cause; a page saying "users are burning the checkout budget at 20x" is a symptom, and it stays correct when the cause next time is something else.

Which brings us to the dashboard. The failure mode is familiar: 60 panels, every metric the service exports, arranged by which team added them. At 03:00 that is unreadable, because you are not browsing, you are answering a fixed sequence of questions.

The SRE book's framing is that monitoring should answer two questions, what is broken and why, and that a dashboard should answer basic questions about your service, normally including the four golden signals: **latency** (time to serve a request, tracked separately for successes and failures), **traffic** (demand, such as requests per second), **errors** (rate of failing requests, explicit, implicit or by policy), and **saturation** (how full the most constrained resource is).

blocks.title: A dashboard laid out as the questions you ask at 03:00

scenes.caption: Eight panels, one question each, read left to right and top to bottom. Nothing here is on the dashboard because a metric exists; each panel is on it because an incident forces that question.
03:12. The page says fast burn. The top-left panel confirms it with the only number that decides whether to escalate: a burn rate of 20 against a threshold of 14.4.
Symptoms next: 2.0 percent of requests are 5xx and p99 has gone from 180 ms to 1.3 s. Now you know what is broken, and the shape (errors and latency together) rules out a pure overload of one route.
Causes next. Latency broken out by downstream shows the orders database at 0.9 s, and the saturation panel shows the connection pool at 100 percent. Two candidates, one of which explains the other.
Always ask what changed. A deploy at 03:04, eight minutes before the page, is the highest-value correlation on any dashboard and the one that most often ends the incident.
Finally the exemplar: click a sample in the slow histogram bucket and land on the trace from lesson 5, which shows one 900 ms query holding the pool. Metrics narrowed it, the trace proved it.

blocks.md:
Three habits make that layout work in practice.

- Put the SLO panel first and give it the alert threshold as a visible line, so the dashboard and the page never disagree.
- Show latency as several quantiles plus the count, never a mean, and remember from lesson 3 that each quantile is only as trustworthy as the nearest bucket boundary.
- Keep the panel count small enough to read in one screen. The SRE book's warning is that teams should avoid any situation where someone must stare at a screen to watch for problems; the dashboard exists for the minutes after a page, not instead of one.

A dashboard is an ordered list of questions, not a list of metrics. Start with the SLO burn rate (are users hurt), then symptoms (what is broken), then causes and changes (why), then one link into a single trace (prove it).

blocks.question: The SLO is 99.9 percent over 30 days. For one hour the error ratio sits at 1.0 percent. How much of the monthly error budget does that hour spend?
options: 0.14 percent
10 percent, because 1 percent is ten times the allowance
1.39 percent
100 percent, since the error ratio exceeded the SLO
blocks.explain: The burn rate is 0.01 / 0.001 = 10, and budget spent is burn rate times window over period: 10 x 1/720 = 1.39 percent, about 36 seconds of the 43.2-minute monthly budget. The 10 percent answer confuses the burn rate with the fraction spent, which would be true only if the hour were the whole window.

blocks.question: Why does the recommended page rule require both a 1-hour and a 5-minute window to exceed the same threshold?
options: The two windows are averaged together to reduce noise
The short window makes the alert stop firing soon after the errors stop, instead of staying lit for an hour
The short window makes the alert fire sooner than the long window alone would
The short window catches a different burn rate from the long one
blocks.explain: A one-hour rate keeps a finished incident above the threshold for most of an hour, so the alert would stay lit long after recovery. Requiring the 5-minute rate too clears it within minutes. Both windows use the same burn-rate threshold, so neither averaging nor a second burn rate is involved.

blocks.question: Which panel earns the top-left corner of an incident dashboard for a user-facing service?
options: Per-pod CPU for all 50 pods
Garbage collection pause times
A heatmap of every internal RPC method's latency
SLO burn rate and error ratio for the user-facing endpoint
blocks.explain: The first question in any incident is whether users are hurt and how fast the budget is draining, which also decides whether to escalate. The other three are cause panels: useful at step three, useless as the first thing you see, and all three can look alarming during a perfectly healthy deploy.
